utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, please have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can everyone hear me? Good morning everyone. The interpreters can hear me, the Defence, the Prosecution, the accused, so we will resume where we left off. Mr. Cayley, we are hearing the testimony of Captain Eric Liebert.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We are, Mr. President, yes. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Captain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning. So we're resuming the examination-in-chief. Mr. Cayley, the witness is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Mr. President. Captain Liebert, good morning, we left off with your testimony yesterday, after a meeting that you attended in the municipality of Zenica with a number of NGO's, and I would like you to now move forward in time to a visit you made to the villages of Rotilj and Visnjica on the 22th of May, 1993, and if you can narrate to the court, what you discovered in the village during that visit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I visited the village of Rotilj and Visnjica again on the 22nd of May. The notes I have from that visit are basically related to some conversations I had with the civilians, the Bosnian Muslim civilians on the ground. The first note here is with respect to their medical needs. The medical situation was not particularly good at that time. They requested a doctor or a nurse to attend to approximately six -- correction, ten sick people. One of those people was a male suffering from an eye problem that could not be dealt with through standard first aid. I also noted comments with respect to patrolling, which I imagine relates to the HVO activity in that area, and some concerns over religious freedom, particularly a concern whether or not the priest that presented their Bajram, and I take that to be their term for Ramadan ceremonies, that priest was apparently from Visnjica, and there was some concern whether he was going to be given access to the Rotilj area. My understanding was that, although the Mosque itself was destroyed, they had set up some kind of makeshift facility to allow them to carry on their religious practices, and they were concerned that they would not be able to fully celebrate their religious ceremonies. That's the limit of my notes on that visit. I would characterise, based on my recollection, the state of mind of the people on the ground there, as basically one of helpless resignation. They had basically come to accept that their lives were going to carry on regardless, and they had come to basically accept the controls that were being placed on them by the HVO authorities, in particular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were these people constituted in the sense of were they mainly males or mainly women and children or young or old?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My recollection of the population in the Rotilj/Visnjica area is basically a population of the elderly. Females, women and children. There were males of military age present, but they were very much in the minority. My understanding is that most of the people meeting that profile, had left during the earlier fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these people constitute a security threat to anybody, in your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw any of these people carrying arms. They, to me, did not constitute a significant security threat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you state that the population was heavily controlled in these two villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would. There were two checkpoints in that immediate area, one that I indicated yesterday, the other one I cannot recall exactly where it was positioned, but basically control into and out of that area or, of movement into and out of that area, was very positive. It was controlled by the HVO. The population itself was contained in the sense that the areas around these villages were populated by Bosnian Croats and that this, in fact, from my perspective, was a hostile civilian population. It would have been very difficult for a person, a Bosnia Muslim civilian living in that vicinity, to move around freely without encountering either HVO soldiers, armed HVO soldiers or a hostile public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move forward to the 30th of May of 1993 when, I think, you received information about activities in the municipality of Kresevo, and I wonder if you could narrate to the court, the information you received in that respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My notes are very brief, but on the 30th of May, I received a report of ethnic cleansing in Kresevo. I don't like that term myself. Basically, what I understood this to mean was that people had been instructed to leave that area, and by people, I mean Bosnian Muslim civilians. I'm not exactly sure who gave me that information. It's not noted here, but that information, based on the way it's presented here, either came to me from one of my liaison officers or was reported by either the HVO or the ABiH military authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware by whom these Bosnian Muslims were being instructed to leave Kresevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no specific notes with respect to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could move forward now to the 1st of June, '93, another of your regular visits to the village of Rotilj. This, I believe, was an unescorted visited in the sense of, unescorted by the HVO. Can you narrate, to the court, what you discovered on this occasion and what you were told by the local villagers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My notes with respect to the 1st of June visit indicate the following. I received reports from the locals, the Bosnian Muslims in that area about bunkers in the hills around Rotilj. I was never able to confirm these reports. There was no system of fortification surrounding those villages. I also had discussions with the people there about what happened during the initial days and how the situation in Rotilj began, and what I was told at that time was that seven people had been killed during the initial attack on the village, and that six people, six members of that village, were still in prison. I took that to be, in prison, somewhere in the Kiseljak area. My other notes, with respect to that visit, are with respect to the condition of the housing and the general state of the villagers. They requested plastic to repair broken windows and help weatherproof some of the damaged houses. They basically stated that aid in any form would be welcome and they indicated that they had last received a ration of basically four kilograms of flour per person approximately 20 days ago. That would indicate to me that they were beginning to have a food problem and that food was not as abundant as it was earlier in my tour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, people spoke more freely to you on this particular visit. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a noticeable difference when I visited this village without an escort. People were much more comfortable talking to me. Generally, more people were interested in talking to me, and their comments were much more to the point. When I was escorted, they were very careful about what they said, and while I can't say there was an evident outright fear, they were obviously very concerned about how their comments would be construed by the people escorting me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people escorting you were generally the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was always escorted by the HVO, when I was escorted in this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try and investigate the allegations that members of the village were being kept in custody by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did try to investigate those allegations. With respect to this particular village, I was not able to identify civilian people in custody in the HVO barracks. We did not have access to all of the areas within the Kiseljak pocket, so we were unable to verify this. I did get verification on other things later, but I think we'll discuss that separately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't have free access within the Kiseljak barracks, to inspect all the areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's very correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move forward to the 15th of June of 1993, to the fall of Kakanj to Bosnian government forces, and I wonder if you can explain to the court your recollection of those events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I believe on the 14th of June or so, the situation in central Bosnia began to change quite radically. By this, I mean there were a series of events which precipitated a significant change in the military situation in my area. On or about the 14th of June, there was an assassination in the area of Kakanj, I believe an Iranian diplomat was assassinated. This action precipitated a conflict between the ABiH and the HVO forces in that area. That conflict basically led to the defeat of HVO forces in that area and a significant population movement to the area of Vares directly to the east, which was under HVO control. The population movement was very large, at least in my experience, roughly 10 to 15,000 people were forced to move to Vares. This was the first, that I'm aware of, major setback for the HVO forces in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you sate that there was this large population movement from Kakanj to Vares. Did one of your liaison officers investigate why this move of population took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This movement of population, this change had very dramatic affects on the ground. As a result of that, there was some concern as to how this came about. One of my liaison officers, a Captain Christian Levesque, conducted a series of interviews with Bosnian Croat displaced people, in the Vares area, after these events had taken place, in an effort to find out exactly what happened and to address some of the allegations that we had received. One of the things that came to his attention in a couple interviews was that there were Bosnian Croat civilians who had indicated that they were forced to leave their houses by the HVO military forces, as they withdrew. Now, I don't believe this to be the case in the overall number, but I do believe that this was a contributing factor to the size of the population displacement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did this large population increase, in Vares, affect conditions in the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions in Vares deteriorated dramatically and very quickly. I visited the area over the next couple days repeatedly in an effort to coordinate emergency assistance to the people involved. Basically, the overall population of Vares, if I recall correctly, was approximately 21,000 people, and to add 10,000 or 15,000 people to this, placed enormous strains on the infrastructure. What immediately happened was a rapid deterioration of basic things like sanitation and health and, indeed, our major concern at this stage was the outbreak of disease. It also placed a tremendous burden on the civil authorities, in terms of controlling that number of upset people, and it placed tremendous strains on the system. We were not set up to feed that many people, in that location. This resulted in a number of things, one of which was the dramatic increase in tension specifically as it released to Bosnian Muslims still residing in that area, and we quickly received several reports of Bosnian Muslims being attacked, either by displaced civilians or displaced soldiers and being force to leave their homes, to make space for displaced families from the Kakanj area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By whom were these Bosnian Muslims being attacked and removed from their homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We received several reports. I believe that the attacks were both from civilians and there was a significant number of actually displaced HVO soldiers. I was given the number 860 soldiers. These soldiers, I believe, were originally from the Travnik area. They had been involved in the fighting in Kakanj and had withdrawn as the situation changed in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe on the 18th of June of 1993, there was another large movement of the population, but this time from Vares itself. If the witness can be shown Exhibit 365? If you could just identify for me -- this is a map that you, in fact, drew for me; is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does the red line indicate -- sorry, the orange line indicate on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This orange line basically is a very rough indication of the line of confrontation or the line separating Bosnian Croat controlled areas from Bosnian Serb controlled areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could just point to the town of Vares?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the town of Vares right there. (indicating)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then if you could narrate to the Court your recollection of this movement of the population on the 18th of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shortly after the events unfolded in the Vares/Kakanj area, it became apparent that there was another population movement in progress. Initially, I received reports from the ABiH authorities in Bisoko that Bosnian Croats were moving through the BSA or Bosnia Serb lines. These reports were later verified both in terms of large numbers of people arriving in Kiseljak and also by the HVO authorities themselves. I believe that authorities in Kiseljak and, as well as, authorities in Vares, and specifically ^ Zvonko Duzunovic, confirmed that this was, in fact, the case. My understanding of what happened was that there was an arrangement made with the Bosnian Serbs, and it was a detailed arrangement negotiated between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Serbs, to permit the movement of people through their area. My understanding is that they facilitated this movement, the Bosnian Serbs facilitated this movement, by providing transport. As I understand it, the movement was through a town in this location called Brgulji and down basically along the area that I've indicated or have had indicated by these blue arrows. Off the map to the south, basically they would connect two major road networks that lead into the Kiseljak area and re-enter Bosnian Croat controlled areas from that direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea of the numbers involved, the movement from Vares to Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were thousands of people involved. The bulk of the 860-some-odd HVO soldiers from the Travnik area moved through this route, as well as thousands of civilians. My understanding is that basically, if we take a look at the number 12,000 to 15,000, if that was the original displaced population from Kakanj, approximately 10 per cent of that population ended up returning to their homes. The remainder, upwards of 10,000 people, were basically redistributed through Vares and Kiseljak. This represented an increase of several thousand people in the Kiseljak area, and this had an affect on the housing demands in that area. Basically, the Bosnian Croat people that had been displaced from Kakanj and who had arrived in Kiseljak demanded a certain level of housing and a certain level of comfort, and obviously, this had a direct effect on the amount of tension between the civilian population, the Bosnian Croat civilians and the Bosnian Muslims, in that area. Housing was very much in demand, and Bosnian Muslims were the easiest source of housing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware as to whether or not any of the Bosnian Croats who had left Kakanj to go to Vares actually returned to Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Can I just ask a question? What do you mean by the "Muslims were the easiest source of housing"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I meant was that there were a lot of things going on in central Bosnia at this time. As I've stated, the military situation was changing quite quickly. It wasn't a good time to start building houses. There were other demands on those resources. So if you're looking for housing, you're going to have to find something from what already exists; and from a Bosnian Croat perspective, given the climate at this time, the most obvious source for new housing is dislocating a Bosnian Muslim that lives in your area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Dislocating them to go where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically kicking them out of their house. "Who cares where they go, as long as I've got a house."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did they still remain in the place or were they kicked out of town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We'll probably get into that in more detail later, sir, but basically forcing them out of their house, and they either have to find somewhere else in the immediate area to live with a relative or in an emergency centre, or they have to leave the area to an area controlled by other forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just returning briefly to the question that I asked you. Are you aware of any Bosnian Croats returning from Vares to Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My understanding is approximately 10 per cent of the overall number did return to Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was a Bosnian government controlled region by this stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could move on now to a period beginning with the 20th of June, 1993, when I think you were involved in a body exchange between the HVO and the ABiH, and I wonder if you could narrate that particular event to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 20th of June, I became aware that the ABiH or Bosnian Muslim forces in the Visoko area had coordinated a body exchange with the HVO forces in the Kiseljak area. At this stage of the conflict and at this stage of my tour, we were avoiding exchanges both in terms of bodies and prisoner exchanges. The reason for that, at least with respect to body exchanges, is that on an earlier exchange or an attempt to recover bodies, some of my officers had been shot at, and it was just considered at this time an unnecessary risk by us, and it was something best left to the combatants to sort out amongst themselves. Now, in this particular case, it was brought to my attention because the Bosnian Muslim forces, the ABiH, made an allegation that the bodies they had recovered from Kiseljak were, indeed, the bodies of people that had been killed in captivity. Now, my understanding was the bodies were recovered the day before, on the 19th of June, and I did not see those bodies until the 20th of June. My understanding from what I was told was that the bodies had been recovered from two separate graves in the Kiseljak civilian cemetery, that basically the bodies had been interned there temporarily until they could be transferred. As soon as I was informed that there was a concern, I immediately made arrangements to deal with this concern and to start documenting events. I returned to the camp in Visoko where I retrieved my own camera and I got another officer or information officer, Lieutenant Ron Vieulleau, to accompany me to the local -- what best could be described as a funeral home. We immediately moved to that location, and that is where I witnessed the seven bodies that had been received by the ABiH forces. Now, these bodies had been buried for maybe up to two weeks in some cases, so there was some decomposition, but for most cases, they were intact and in fairly good shape. What was immediately apparent and what happened, I basically went through body by body as the -- I wouldn't call them a coroner, but as the Bosnian Muslim funeral director described the injuries, and this was basically passed to me through my interpreter, and I basically visually inspected each of the bodies as their wounds were described to me. And at the time, I tried to take notes and take photographs to document this. Lieutenant Vieulleau was with me the whole time as a second set of eyes, basically. The one thing that was immediately apparent and of concern to me was the fact that most of these individuals had massive head injuries, visibly crushed skulls in some cases. Several of them also had other wounds, but the head injuries themselves were a concern.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can interrupt you, Captain Liebert? Mr. President, there are a series of 12 extremely unpleasant photographs, which I don't intend to show, but there are two photographs which the witness has identified to me demonstrate what he is talking about. So if those two photographs could be placed on the ELMO, that's 366 and 367, I think that will assist in his testimony, and we can move forward through this quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please go on, Mr. Cayley. We have here -- the other photographs, I assume, will also be tendered, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I didn't intend to tender them, Mr. President. They don't demonstrate anything more than these photographs, but I'll allow my learned friend to inspect them, if he wishes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain Liebert, if you could continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't intend to dwell on this for too long. These photographs are representative of the ones taken. Things that concerned me at the time were the fact that many of these people had noticeable, sizeable head wounds, that I would characterise in some cases as crushing injuries or blunt force injuries. There was also indications, like this man here, of what appeared to me -- and I'm not a doctor -- as signs of beating, and in the case here, this corpse had been burnt. Now, I didn't deal with large numbers of bodies and that's basically all I have to show for that, so if we can turn the ELMO off?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those photographs can be removed now from the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Was there a medical report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. I never dealt with a situation of this nature before and, as such, I didn't call upon doctors immediately to get involved. I did show the photographs, the developed photographs, to a surgeon, a Canadian Forces surgeon, and explained my concerns to him, and he indicated that, in his view -- and he couldn't give a final conclusion because he was not there -- but in his view, the photographs did lead him to have cause that something was not right here. My concern, as I expressed to him, that there had been a crime committed and that it is possible that these people did not die on the battlefield but they died in captivity and that they had possibly died as the result of torture. The surgeon, a Major Raza Mahran (phoen), took a look at my photographs and said, yes, he would share those concerns based on what he saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these were Bosnian prisoners of war; was that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding is that they were Bosnian Muslims, and the reason why I expressed these concerns is that the head injuries, in particular, were not representative of injuries that one would sustain on a Bosnian battlefield. It didn't matter which opposing force you were dealing with. In the context of this civil war, hand-to-hand combat was uncommon, and to see so many casualties all suffering from head wounds was extremely unusual and was of great cause of concern to me. It led me to believe that something was not right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you approached the HVO about your concerns, what did they say to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent the next week or so basically travelling back and forth between the two sides trying to prepare a report and trying to document this incident. The HVO, in particular, I think, Vinko Lucic, was the man I talked to the most on this subject, provided me two different stories. Initially, when I expressed the concern that these people had not died in combat, they said, "Oh, yes, they had died indeed on the battlefield." Later, when I pushed them on this subject, they said, Well, perhaps the injuries that I had noted had been caused when the bodies were disinterred, dug up. I had difficulty believing either of those stories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this exchange took place in the HVO headquarters in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is, in fact, correct. Just for the record, there was a similar allegation made, reference the single body that had been recovered by the Bosnian Croats. I never did get a chance to see that body because they had reburied the individual before I could take a look at him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move ahead in time now to the 22nd, 23rd of June, 1993, when I think you had reason to visit a number of Bosnian Muslim civilians that were being held at the council building in Kiseljak. I wonder if you can explain to the Court what happened on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. As I've stated before, at this particular period of my tour, I was travelling back and forth between Visoko and Kiseljak almost daily, basically dealing with different allegations and different concerns. On approximately the 22nd of June, the commanding officer of the ABiH forces in Visoko made a report to me about people who had arrived in Visoko from Kiseljak, and their concern, in particular, was with respect to the villages of Radanovici and ^ Pelska Kuprija, both villages in the Kiseljak area, and how women and children in those villages had been -- men, women and children in those villages, had been rounded up and removed, and that some of them were being held in the council building. There were also allegations that the men were being forced to dig trenches and that civilians were being held in a building near the football stadium in Kresevo. Obviously, these were fairly serious accusations in our mind, and I speak from the CANBAT 2 perspective, so this was immediately addressed with the HVO authorities in Kiseljak. On the 23rd of June, at 11.05 hours, I had a meeting with Vinko Lucic in the HVO barracks in Kiseljak, and his response with respect to the two villages I've named was that inquiries did happen, that basically meaning that the men had been collected, that the families probably came along to ensure the safety of their men, and that women, children and some men were released. Other men have since been released because these inquiries took some time. Then they made the general statement that all men in Kiseljak have been mobilised, that Bosnian Muslims do not bear arms so they are used for other jobs, and at this time, he used the example that they could be used for baking bread. Now, there were people in the council building, and I don't have notes about exactly when I visited them, but at the time I visited the council building, there were approximately 60 to 70 people living there. I would characterise that facility as being used as some kind of transit centre, basically being used to house people that had been removed from their houses for whatever reason and shelter them while alternate arrangements were made. In the case of people in the council building, I later met people that were held there living with relatives elsewhere in Kiseljak. And that's all I've got to say on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the people that were held in the council building, they were Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all of these facilities were under the control of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO and the local civilian authorities, so the mayor of Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when Mr. Lucic told you that Bosnian Muslims were being used to bake bread, what did you think about that explanation of what was taking place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I would take as sort of a good example of the flippant remarks that I experienced when I was dealing with these people. I did not take that to mean that they were employed as bakers in the literal sense. I construed that as some kind of joke in relation to my questions with respect to whether they had been used for digging trenches or fortifications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can now move ahead in time to the 25th of June, 1993 when I think you interviewed a woman in Duhri?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. There were a number of developments in the Kiseljak area at this time. I've already indicated that there was significant population movement. There was also some activity in the eastern edge of what we would call the Kiseljak pocket, and there had been reports of gunfire in the area of Han Ploca, in particular. I received a report of mistreatment and, in fact, I was told that a Bosnian Muslim girl had been raped by HVO soldiers. Taking my lessons from the body exchange incident, I immediately tried to find this individual, and when I did locate her, I made sure that I had a medical officer present with me when I conducted the interview. When I conducted this interview, and I believe it was conducted in the village of Duhri, there was a Major Cote, one of our medical officers, present. Basically, the notes that I made from my individual, I believe the individual I interviewed was named Fatima. I can't remember what her last name was. Her account basically was as follows: On the 15th of June, 1993, she was living in her village, a village called Grahovici -- it's near Han Ploca -- when there was a combined HVO-Bosnian Serb attack on that area. She, with about 15 other people, escaped and spent three days in the woods before they got hungry and had to return for food, and the town was still quite active at that time. She was accompanied by an old man from Tulica. I believe that's the name of it. It was a village burnt the day before. Together, they were told to surrender and led, basically, home. Fatima and an old woman stayed behind to take care of the cattle, and basically she called out for her mother but nothing happened. There were approximately 30 BSA and HVO soldiers who were in the area. They stopped by her house and started to question her and the people with her, such as, "Where is your father?" "Who is the commanding officer of the ABiH forces?" Did they know where these people were? Fatima was then told to shoot at some of her relatives, and the troops forced a weapon into her hands and fired a couple of shots into the ground. A man she identified by his nickname, Firka (phoen), an HVO soldier, told her to open her mouth and placed his gun in her mouth. He wanted to take her to the stable and claimed he was going to rape her. Two of the soldiers with him, identified as Croats, told him to let her go and used force to remove her from his custody. She was then taken to the same building as the rest, she says. That was a stable. A neighbour of hers was killed, and she was told to relax. She was told that Firka was also killed. There were more shots fired. Eventually, what happened is these individuals were taken over the mountains and, through force, by foot to a village called Drazevici where they were placed on an HVO truck and brought to the Kiseljak barracks where they were given food, water and proper treatment. On the 17th of June, they were brought to a former elementary school where she was placed with many of the people from her own village. There were more displaced people arriving. They were brought to the council building, where the living conditions weren't particularly good, to the school, back to the council buildings. In total, they ended up spending a fair amount of time there. That's basically how that -- those notes taper off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after this time, did you have occasion to see the villages of Han Ploca and Grahovici from the main road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I drove by those villages each time I went down to Sarajevo, and the villages were obviously damaged, the bulk of that damage, obviously due to burning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me for a second. Did you finish the story of the rape of Fatima? Because up until now, she's not raped.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. She was not, in fact, raped. She had been, from what I could determine, assaulted, but she had not sexually assaulted. She had been manhandled, but there was nothing there to constitute what I would call a rape. Her treatment certainly was unacceptable, but my initial concerns about the rape were not founded and there was no need for a medical examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we can move back to Rotilj for a final time, and I would like you to describe to the Court how conditions were in that village by September-October of 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Haven't we covered that already, Mr. Cayley? Please try to be a bit more concise. We've treated Rotilj, haven't we, the area of concentration of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the significant part of this witness's testimony is that he visited the village over a number of months, and he saw conditions change, deteriorate, get considerably worse. Now he will finally address the Court on how he saw Rotilj towards the end of the tour. It is an important part of the proof for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. It's absolutely your right. What I would like to ask the witness is to try and synthesise a little; often you go into detail. We didn't know whether the woman was raped or not raped. Because we have already heard a summary of your testimony. You are not a witness like others. You're an intelligent witness; not like others who were victims who are facing a tribunal for the first time. You're a senior officer. So I would like to ask you to concentrate on the questions that are being asked and to answer them; otherwise, we will be repeating the same things, because we already know a lot since the beginning of this trial last June. It is the right of Mr. Cayley to ask you questions, but it is the right of the judges to have synthesised and focused answers. Mr. Cayley, please put your questions well, without excessive digression.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain Liebert, if you can narrate to the Court how you saw the final conditions in the village of Rotilj at the end of your tour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I have notes here from two more visits to that area. The ones I'm referring to right now are from the 28th of September. At that time, I visited the area of Rotilj-Visnjica. There were, in addition to the people that lived there when I visited earlier in my tour, approximately 600 displaced people from all over the Kiseljak area. Specifically, the people I was talking to were from Visnjica, Doci, Han Ploca, Duhri, Grahovici. I would characterise Rotilj and the surrounding area as a concentration point at that time in that the population, the Bosnian Muslim population from the surrounding areas, had been concentrated in that area. Basically, they were still living in the same 15 to 20 houses that the original inhabitants were residing in when I first started visiting. By this stage of the game, there were electricity problems throughout central Bosnia, and indeed this area had no electricity. Conditions were not at all good. There was mounting concern on our part that these people would not be able to survive the winter without extreme suffering and, perhaps, death. There were food shortages being experienced throughout central Bosnia, but, in particular, this area was of extreme concern because of the way these people were living. Many of them were exposed to the elements. The area they were living in was very overcrowded, and we also had some health concerns because of this overcrowding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it would be right to say that conditions were considerably worse than when you had first visited the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can now move forward? Specifically, the HVO chain of command from Kiseljak to Vares. How would you regard the quality of that chain of command, and if you can give specific examples to the Court to support any claim you might make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would regard the chain of command between Kiseljak and Vares to be extremely effective. The passage of information was good. There was no problems there. They were able to move freely between those two locations by way of the Bosnian Serb lines. The information that I would receive in either location basically lined up. There was very good evidence that the passage of information was efficient, and they were able to coordinate their activities. The best example I can think of was the capture of the commanding officer of the ABiH forces in Visoko, a man by the name of Mimisevic, who was captured in Vares and eventually detained down in the Kiseljak area. He was captured en route to visit his family in Tuzla. He was intercepted in the Vares area, and subsequently passed, I assume, by way of the Bosnian Serb lines to the forces in Kiseljak, and that is where I next saw him in the custody of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you saw Mr. Rajic give orders to his subordinates, did those subordinates always obey him, from what you could see in the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, yes. He seemed to be exercising effective control over his subordinates, and when he issued direction, it was complied with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown the next exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned that this Bosnian commander was subsequently passed through the Bosnian Serb lines to the forces of Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So what is cooperation? Cooperation between the Bosnian Croats and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had ample evidence of very close coordination and cooperation between the HVO forces, the Bosnian Croat forces, and the Bosnian Serb forces in our area. I was led to believe they were also receiving some support in the form of supplies as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown the next exhibit, please? Now, Captain Liebert, I believe the orange and blue lines represent a route that you took on a number of occasions between Visoko and Fojnica, the orange route being the first route that you took and then upper portion of road controlled by the Bosnian government forces, and then down the blue road to Fojnica. Are you aware that that section of road where you've marked in two Bosnian checkpoints was controlled by Bosnian government forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The area, basically between these two green marks, was controlled by the ABiH or Bosnian government forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the areas either side of those checkpoints was controlled by the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a bit of a no man's land and then you would find HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, as it were, the checkpoint to the right, that moves down towards Kiseljak, and the checkpoint on the left is up towards Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is, indeed, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you believe, or if you could explain to the Court, whether or not the ground between these two checkpoints was, in fact, permeable either by an individual or a small force so as to enable somebody to travel between Busovaca and Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I first arrived in this area in May, the area of Fojnica, which is down here to the left, was basically a neutral area. In fact, the headquarters in Kiseljak, the UN headquarters in Kiseljak, called it the peace zone or zone of special interest. So there was no fighting in here, and basically, although there was tension, Bosnian Croat and Bosnian Muslim people were living together. Eventually that came to an end when there was fighting in the area, and Kiseljak was physically separated from Busovaca. Now, I travelled down this road marked in blue, the Kacuni-Fojnica road, several times, generally when my access to Fojnica was cut off by the HVO, and I got a chance to see firsthand what that country is like. Basically, what you're talking about is a fairly rough terrain, not what I would call mountainous, but very hilly, treed and sparsely populated. And what this means is that if I had to move between Kiseljak and Busovaca, it would be fairly easy to do so, given the force that was on the ground. It's very difficult to see very far because of all the trees and the rough terrain. It's very difficult to maintain supervision on that area. So I would say that from a military perspective, in my professional opinion, this area is porous, i.e., if I wanted to move a small force, let's say up to a platoon size, through this area, I would be fairly confident that I could do so without being prevented or stopped along the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where were the bulk of the Bosnian government forces patrolling this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my experience, and this is just travelling along here, basically you've got men at the checkpoint, you've got men in the Kacuni area, you've got men in the Bilalovac area -- that's probably where the bulk of the forces in this area are -- and men at this checkpoint. The forces themselves are basically concentrated on the road and in major population areas, the villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the largest number of soldiers that you ever saw, Bosnian Muslim solders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing a force any larger than a platoon moving along the road in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many soldiers is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe 30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you see any evidence during your time in Kiseljak of military coordination between the headquarters in Vitez and the HVO headquarters in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I don't have any direct evidence, I did not see people on a radio or at the other end of a fax machine, but what I did see was the -- what I would say was symptomatic of an effective chain of command and communication system. In the fall of 1993, there were a number of evacuations of a medical facility in Nova Bila, which is off in the British area of responsibility near Vitez. This was basically an HVO field hospital, it was very much a makeshift affair, and as the casualties mounted, they needed some place to evacuate these people to because they were rudimentary medical facilities. The nearest decent hospital that was capable of dealing with excess casualties was in Kiseljak, in our area of control. So there were a number of evacuations under the name "Op.," "Operation Finlay," that basically resulted in the transfer of casualties over land, under UN military escort, from the British area of responsibility through to Kiseljak in our area of responsibility. The only coordination problems we really experienced with those transfers were problems between UNPROFOR and the HVO. The HVO activities were very well-coordinated, and, in fact, I seem to recall the fact that casualties were actually evacuated from the Kiseljak area to other facilities by helicopter. That kind of activity had to be coordinated and generally requires a fairly good communication system to effect successfully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an HVO helicopter landing zone in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They used the sports field in Kiseljak for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, finally, Captain Liebert, if you could just sum up succinctly the policy of the HVO that you observed taking place in Kiseljak and Vares during your tour in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no direct evidence that the HVO carried out a deliberate programme against the Bosnian Muslim civilian population in those areas; however, I would describe their approach, at very best, as being an almost criminal indifference. And I don't choose those words lightly. I believe that the chain of command was negligent in exercising their responsibilities of command; that Mr. Rajic, in particular, set a very poor example for his subordinates to follow; that the negative opinions held by Mr. Rajic were shared by many of his staff, and that they openly expressed those views in the form of jokes and comments basically which indicated to me a lack of concern for the Muslim population in their areas. I believe that this had a direct effect on the situation on the ground, and if it did not contribute to the harsh treatment of people in that area, it definitely didn't improve the situation at all. I believe that a responsible military commander with the force available to intervene should have exercised his responsibilities to provide some level of protection for those people. What was happening to them was obvious, it was obvious to me, and I feel that the fact that the HVO did not intervene in any way and may have contributed to the situation was a failure of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The previous map that the witness referred to in respect of the Kacuni-Bilalovac road is Exhibit 368, I believe. I have no further questions for the witness. If I could apply for admission of all of the exhibits, which, I think, number from 362 through to 368?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see that there are no objections by the counsel. We shall now take a 20-minute break and then we shall begin our cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I assume it's Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you and good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The HVO officers with whom you had contact, I take it, were Ivica Rajic and the subordinate chain of command below him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever met or seen Colonel Blaskic prior to entering the courtroom yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say that, in your opinion, the chain of command in the HVO was negligent in exercising the responsibilities of command, are you referring to those officers with whom you had contact, Ivica Rajic and below?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Specifically, I'm referring to those individuals; however, in the Canadian understanding of how military operations work, we have a saying that you can delegate authority, but you cannot delegate your responsibility. What that means is, I can delegate the authority for a specific operation, but I am still responsible for exercising that supervisory role inherent in command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you speak of responsibility in that context, you were talking about military responsibility, not criminal responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm talking about military responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say certain persons in your view conducted themselves with criminal indifference towards the plight of Muslims, for instance, in the Kiseljak municipality, you are not including Colonel Blaskic, the then Colonel Blaskic in the opinion you're rendering; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That opinion is expressed specifically for the individuals that I dealt with. Now, it's my understanding that Mr. Blaskic filled a senior position and, therefore, had the responsibilities inherent in that senior position, but I did not specifically deal with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, when you speak of responsibilities, you're speaking of military responsibilities, not specific responsibilities that may exist under international humanitarian or international criminal law; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm speaking military responsibilities, specifically the responsibility for the actions of the subordinates underneath you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which, in strict military parlance, that's a strict liability. You can delegate something, but you can't delegate responsibility in the military sense; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're not able to give any further opinions as to my client, General Blaskic, because, for example, would you agree, you have never seen any reports that he may have received from the Kiseljak municipality, from the HVO in Kiseljak; correct? You've never seen any such reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no direct observations of that relationship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've never seen any orders that General Blaskic may have given or attempted to give to the HVO in the Kiseljak municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you clarify your relationship with Captain Lanthier, with whom I take it there was a common period of service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I first arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina in early May of 1993, Captain Lanthier was the military affairs liaison officer, his specific responsibilities being contact with the opposing factions. He returned to the Bosnia-Herzegovina theatre of operations in November, 1993 where he was employed as the senior liaison officer and became, in fact, my counterpart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it he left when you arrived; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when he returned, were you colleagues working on the same -- in the same activities, or what was your relationship with him after he returned to the theatre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He spent approximately about two weeks in theatre with me at the end of my tour where we did a detailed handover, where I handed over my duties and responsibilities, made sure he was well-briefed on the situation as it pertained to operations at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any of your discussions with him, did he tell you what position he understood Vinko Lucic to hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall a specific discussion with Jean Mark Lanthier. My understanding of Mr. Lucic's position is based, in most part, with my dealings with the man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked yesterday in your testimony about the ways in which CANBAT, the Canadian battalion, communicated and carried out its functions in Visoko and Srebrenica, two locations separated by some distance. You discussed the use of a radio to maintain communications between those units. Can you tell us what kind of radios your battalion had available to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially, the radio we used was an AN 515 high frequency radio. That's the radio we use for long-distance communications because it was most suitable for the terrain we found in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We also later on, and the radio I personally used was of civilian pattern CODAN HF radio which was smaller and more modern. The radio technology the Canadian Armed Forces was using dated back to the 1960's. The CODAN radio was a commercially available radio which was much more modern and much more reliable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it the AN 515 high frequency radio was not particularly reliable in that theatre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was reliable, but like any older piece of technology it had seen better days. It didn't have the benefits of computerisation, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No digital tuning and that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what types of radios were available in the supplies of the former Yugoslav National Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have very little firsthand knowledge of the Yugoslav communication systems and do not have any specific recollection of communications equipment being held by any of the opposing factions. I did not witness anybody handling any communication equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The communications equipment that CANBAT had, and I don't want you to disclose anything that may be sensitive to your government, but were they or did they include secure forms of communication, as in encrypted communications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did have that capability. We did not, as a rule, use that capability because the UN, by and by, frowns on the use of coded communications. We try to be as open as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with the proposition that for warring parties, the security of their communications is of critical importance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a general military rule, that is the case. You don't need technology to achieve that, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you spoke of command being exercised from Visoko by CANBAT over CANBAT in Srebrenica and you also spoke of your experiences in Cyprus. First let me ask you about Cyprus and then I have some general questions. When you were in Cyprus you were there as a peacekeeper; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is in fact correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's also true of your tour of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our role in Bosnia-Herzegovina was somewhat different. The mandate was completely different. We weren't actually peacekeeping because there was no peace at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there peace or a cease-fire in effect in Cyprus while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I pause after your answers, it's to allow the interpreters to complete their interpretation. Is it true then that in both Cyprus and in Bosnia-Herzegovina the presence of CANBAT was pursuant to an international mandate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that by contrast, the situation in which General Blaskic found himself was that he was a member of a warring party actively engaged in combat on the terrain; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that's an accurate description of the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, indeed, if he had been apprehended or, shall we say, ambushed by the BiH army, the best scenario is he would be captured and imprisoned; the worst scenario is, of course, that he would have been killed on the spot, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That sounds reasonable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Canadian battalion have armoured, armoured personnel carriers or some kind of armoured vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We had two forms of armoured vehicle. We had the M-113, armoured personnel carrier, it's an American vehicle, tracked. We also had what we call a Cougar, fire-support vehicle. It is a wheeled vehicle with a turret and a 76-millimetre gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these used on these trips from Visoko to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally, the trips from Visoko to Srebrenica did include those vehicles, but they were mixed convoys, and the convoy included things like unprotected ambulances, fuel bowser, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The armoured carriers I take it would go along for protection, among other things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The armoured carriers were an inherent part of our rifle companies. They are used as a -- or potentially could be used as a weapon system in themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last question in this area. You said in Cyprus travel at night was difficult because of checkpoints. Was travel by day when you were in Cyprus possible for UN personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was a lot easier because you could approach checkpoints with an expectation that the people manning those checkpoints would be awake. There was no real danger during the day that you would accidentally be engaged by security at those checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have been able to give a lot of detailed testimony due to your notes. Let me ask you about your first visit to the Kiseljak barracks, which you described yesterday in your testimony. You weren't able or you did not give a date for that visit. Are you able to give us a date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've reviewed my notes. I can't -- my notes weren't purpose written, and so I don't have a specific recollection of who was present or the actual timing of that visit. These notes were originally created to refresh my memory on key points.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mentioned Vinko Lucic a moment ago. Do you remember who introduced him to you and how he was introduced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have been introduced to Mr. Lucic as part of my handover. I don't recall who was present at that particular introduction, but very early in my tour I would have met both Mr. Lucic and Mr. Rajic in the Kiseljak HVO barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn that Mr. Lucic had later acted on behalf of the HVO in certain meetings in Sarajevo conducted in August of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I remember Mr. Lucic representing the HVO as part of a delegation to a series of meetings that we called the mixed military working group. These meetings were held in Sarajevo, and the meetings that I attended happened on the 14th and the 18th of August, if I recall correctly. I believe there were also other senior members of the HVO forces present. If I remember correctly, Mr. Pekovic was present at at least one of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you estimate how many times you visited the Kiseljak barracks during your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot provide a firm number. I would guess in excess of 20-some-odd visits probably, during the course of my tour, maybe more, maybe less. My responsibilities did not focus on military affairs. I had a liaison officer designated to do that, so these visits were basically conducted either while that officer was on leave to address more serious matters or to coordinate my movements throughout the area, because there were restrictions placed on our movement, although theoretically, that was not to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already said you never saw Colonel Blaskic in the theatre. Were you ever told during any of your 20 or more visits to the Kiseljak barracks that Colonel Blaskic was in the barracks there in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall that being the case. I don't remember seeing Mr. Blaskic. My understanding of his position is based, in most part, with my -- or on my relationship with the British battalion and my work with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Ivica Rajic and others you named exhibited, through their comments, an apparent indifference or even disregard for the welfare of Muslims in the Kiseljak municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your tour of duty, did anyone in BRITBAT or otherwise, tell you of a personal conversation that they had or had had with Colonel Blaskic in which he exhibited any such disregard for the welfare of persons of Muslim background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall a specific report that would have related specifically to Mr. Blaskic and his attitude towards Muslim civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have talked about the CANBAT experience in central Bosnia. Let me pursue one additional line of inquiry here. Do you know how many officers with formal military education, that is, military academy training there were within the command structure of CANBAT in your tour. Just an estimate is what I'm looking for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That figure would be probably, you're talking military college background?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Military academy, formal military training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of our officers had formal military training. We're a professional force and that is part of the career development of our officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many officers would there have been within CANBAT with that professional military training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but was that 100, 200, and what was the size of the overall force, if you're permitted to tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our battle group was approximately, and these are rough figures, approximately 1,200 personnel, all told, that's non-commissioned officers and soldiers. The number of officers commanding that battle group probably numbered about 40 or so. We also had specialists with us in the form of surgeons, nurses, et cetera, so those numbers may have increased to maybe 60.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know is that consistent with NATO norms if it is a norm you can speak of with respect to NATO generally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It really isn't a NATO norm, it's normal for Canadian forces and was similar to the organisation of the British battalion on our flank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday in your testimony that it can be usual for a force to become separated from a main headquarters in military operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My understanding of military history indicates that's the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that it is not normal, but rather it is extraordinary for a commander in wartime to have command over a large number of separated enclaves, as many as five, six or more, which remain separated over an extended period of time, close to a year's time. Would you agree that that's not normal, that presents a rather extraordinary situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A difficult situation, yes; extraordinary, no. The Germans and Japanese faced similar problems in the second world war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do any Canadian commanders who have ever commanded forces in six or more enclaves over a year's time in combat; do any examples come to mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no immediate examples I can think of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if it occurred within the Canadian military, the situation I've described would be the first, to your knowledge, that it had ever occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In modern history, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yourself, have you had any combat experience, other than as a peacekeeper in Cyprus, and as a member of the United Nations protection force in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Negative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned briefly the commander of the HVO brigade in Fojnica, and I believe you said, to your knowledge, it was Branko Stanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if my memory serves me correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that position change over your tour; that is, did the brigade commander -- if indeed Mr. Stanic was the commander, and I'm not suggesting to you that he was although that is your testimony -- did that position change over at any time during your tour, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm recollecting events that are approximately five years old. I cannot recall a change in command. The situation did change on the ground, so that may have happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If Exhibit 363 could be placed back on the ELMO, that's the chart of certain commanders. And if the ELMO can be activated, please. Perhaps the picture could be enlarged slightly. Drawing your attention to Emil Harik who is indicated on Exhibit 363 as, I believe, a commander or officer in Vares for the HVO. You described him as a moderate. Can you give us an example of moderation in his views?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm just trying to recollect specific examples here. I find it difficult to recollect a specific case; however, based on my discussions with Mr. Harik, and I may have met him maybe three or four occasions total, based on the way he presented himself, how he discussed the opposing forces in the areas adjoining his, based on his responses to concerns that were expressed by myself and others, that's where I formulated the opinion that I have formulated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you draw the conclusion from your meetings with him that he attempted to maintain a positive relationship with the BiH army forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my understanding. It's basically my understanding that this was not particularly unusual, considering that the area to his north was an area where HVO and ABiH forces were openly cooperating in preparing a defence against the Serbs. So he was, from what I could determine, basically occupying a moderate situation, based on the military threat to his area and based on, I guess, his personal relationships with commanders in the areas around his.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did Commander Harik remain in his position as the HVO brigade commander in Vares until sometime after the massacre in Stupni Do in October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on Exhibit 363 on the far right of the exhibit, there's the name of another man, Mr. Duznovic, and the indication on the chart is chain of command unclear. Could you describe -- first of all, strike that. Mr. Duznovic, did you see him in the company of his own force or unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he had his own, what I would describe, as a retinue. He had a security detachment, a fairly small one, that were dressed differently, visibly differently than the HVO forces in the area. Their uniform differed in that they tended to wear more black and they carried sidearms and weapons that were not typical of those carried by the HVO forces in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they better equipped in terms of having superior weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not describe them as necessarily better equipped, but the weaponry was different. The prevalent arm in this area was the Yugoslav version of an AK-47 which is an assault rifle. These individuals were armed with sidearms, and although I do not recall specifically the type of sidearm they were carrying, their weapons and the webbing or equipment that they wore was notably different from those carried by the local HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that suggest to you that their logistics supply line was something different than the rank and file in Vares?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What it suggested to me was that I was dealing with a separate organisation and, as my diagram here indicates, I was not clear as to what their relationship was to the chain of command. My understanding of Zvonko Duznovic's, as a very minimum he was an equal to Emil Harik, in terms of the authority that he exercised, and that he answered to probably somebody in a more senior position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say "an equal" as in "an" equal or unequal, "un"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An equal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was an equal to Mr. Harik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If true, that would give you a situation in Vares where you have two persons within the Bosnian Croat camp of equal and power of influence with chains of command leading not to the same person or persons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know where this particular chain of command led to. They had different areas of responsibility, and Emil Harik's concerns were basically focused on the defence of the Vares area and that's how he comported himself, that's how he controlled his soldiers to the best of my understanding. Zvonko's position was somewhat different. His focus was on the control of the civilian people within that area and his specific interest, at least as it affected my operations, was the control of our access into and out of the areas inhabited by Muslim civilians within Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wouldn't that distinction commonly be referred to as external security versus internal security; namely, Mr. Harik was responsible for external security of the enclave, whereas Mr. Duznovic appeared to you to be responsible for internal security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That seems to be an accurate description of the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is an accurate description?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever learn whether Mr. Duznovic was affiliated with the military police or an intelligence organisation or some other organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe, if I recall correctly, he did have a working relationship with Mr. Rajic. I don't recall any specific examples of that. That's just a general recollection. I don't recall any other special relationships within the HVO chain of command. This was a unique situation with respect to the Canadian area of responsibility and basically was dealt with as such by us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it then you're not suggesting, in any way to the Judges that Mr. Duznovic was the representative of Colonel Blaskic in Vares?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no evidence to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have no basis for any such claim; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last question on this issue. Did you ever learn any information that would tend to inform you whether Mr. Duznovic, his line of command, led to Kiseljak, to Mostar, or to somewhere else, or are you unable to tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm unable to tell you. That's why it's indicated as such, chain of command unclear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience. I'm through with that line of inquiry. You've described the Kiseljak headquarters as well-organised and as a normal set-up. In support of that, you described the escorts that took you in and the fact there was a staff. Are there any other facts or factors that you can draw upon to tell the court why you have the opinion that the Kiseljak headquarters was "normal" and well organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My observations were basically based on my visits to that facility. That facility had included a rifle range, a firing range in the back, from what I heard, was being used while I was there. Therefore, I would conclude that military training was ongoing, at least that's the most positive conclusion I could make, and basically, it was organised much like a barracks -- I would expect a barracks to be organised, under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, indeed, your understanding was that it had been the JNA barracks in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where Ivica Rajic got his orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do I have firsthand information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you personally know where his orders came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not witness Mr. Rajic receiving orders and have no evidence in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Returning for a moment to Mr. Duznovic in Vares, can you think of any parallel or comparable situation in the Canadian army where you might have two persons of equal authority of different lineage or different lines of commands above them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are all kinds of examples of that. Different brigade commanders occupy the same level of authority, obviously, for different groups of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But would you agree, where you have different lines of command over commanders in the same area, it's very important that the duties between those two commanders be clearly differentiated and separated; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is, indeed, the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because if they are not, would you agree you likely will have confusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not just my opinion, it's my understanding. I've seen that happen firsthand. For example, during our emergency operations during the ice storm in Quebec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can have confusions if you have multiple lines of authority, over the same duties in the same area; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can also have inconsistency, inconsistent conduct; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're implying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can have people doing different things, indeed things that may conflict, because there are multiple and different lines of commands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
