utterances.text: Was there any industry located in your Dzemat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no industry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any military facilities located within your Dzemat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, very briefly and succinctly, could you tell the Judges what your duties and responsibilities were within the Dzemat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as a religious person, I was in charge of the religious life of the people in my Dzemat. I was able, during the day, to communicate with people five times by prayer, and I also was able to communicate with peoples from my Dzemat on Fridays during the Bajram, and we had special communication, we had in the mosque which was built in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you became quite familiar with the members of your Dzemat. You knew them well, you socialised with them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to direct your attention to the time frame before the HVO attacked your Dzemat in August of 1992. Can you tell the Judges in your own words whether there are any military targets in the Dzemat and can you describe for the Judges what, if any, weapons were possessed by the Muslim people who lived within the Dzemat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were no military targets in my Dzemat. As far as weapons are concerned, there were basically light infantry weapons, small arms, automatic machine guns, semi-automatics and I left this when I went to get my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say that there were weapons, basically light infantry weapons, small arms, automatic and semi-automatic weapons, were those weapons that were in the village or are those weapons that are formerly in the village but were at the front-line positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, some of the weapons were on the front-line, but the weapons I mentioned were arms used by the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many police were there in your village, in your Dzemat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, not very many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any units of the Bosnian army located in your Dzemat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were no units. The units of the army were in Koscani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you weren't present during the attack on your village that occurred in August of 1992; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you returned, did you have an opportunity to see the damage that had been inflicted as a result of that attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw what had happened. Some houses were burnt down, some stables. I saw a man with crutches, Salem Mujic, who was injured during the attack. I also learned that in that conflict, Mutap Hasan was killed while he was trying to put out the fire on his house and stable. And Zahid Hadzic was also killed when he saw that his stable was on fire. He wished to release the cattle, and then he was shot to death and also a Croat was killed from Potkraj, his name was Luka. That Croat was slightly mentally retarded. He used to come to visit us often. He was a friend with Zahid Hadzic and probably when he saw him shot down, he tried to approach him, but then he was killed on that occasion. And that is what I learned what had happened during that attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges whether the damage that you saw in your Dzemat was exclusively limited to Muslim houses and buildings, or was there also damage done to Croat buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, passing through Potkraj, you must, if you go from the main road you have to first pass through the Croatian dwelling, then a Muslim dwelling. I did not notice any damage to the Croat buildings, but many of the facades were destroyed on the Muslim houses by the shrapnel. My home was also damaged, destroyed, some glass was broken and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the mosque in Topola or the Mektab in Topola damaged as a result of that attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the Minaret was damaged in several points, the facade from several bullets and also there were bullet holes on the Mektab as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the time you returned to Duhri in November, 1992 until the attacks on the villages of Rotilj and Svinjarevo on the 18th of April, 1993, can you describe to the Judges what life was like for the Muslims in your Dzemat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From November, 1992 until the events of April, '93, generally speaking, life was more or less normalised, people could move around fairly freely but there was also the danger that someone might be robbed or looted at the checkpoints which were located at the entrance to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to April 18th, 1993, that is, when the attacks on Rotilj and the other villages occurred. First of all, could you see those attacks taking place or some of those attacks taking place from your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we could not see the attacks directly. We could hear the shooting and we could see the smoke from the burnt buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you subsequently informed about the resulting damage to Muslim religious sites as a result of that fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that the mosque was damaged in Kiseljak, in Gromiljak and also many Muslim houses had been damaged, that some Muslims had been able to move, escape to the territories under the army of the BiH control. Some Muslims hid with their relatives. Some were killed. Some were captured. And this is what I had heard that had happened in that location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before the attacks of the 18th of April, how many Imams were there in the Kiseljak municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, seven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After those attacks, Mr. Dozic, how many Imams remained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A few days after the attack, there was only myself left and Omer Efendija from Han Ploca who was killed in an attack which occurred on June 12th in Han Ploca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following those particular attacks and up to the point in time when the village of Tulica, Han Ploca and Grahovica were attacked, that is around the 12th of June, 1993, can you tell the Judges what happened to the people in your Dzemat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the events which took place in Rotilj, Gromiljak, Visnjica, panic broke out amongst the members of my Dzemat, and people from the experience of August, '92, tried to remove their women and children to the Bosnian territory. Some were successful. There was assistance by friends, Croat friends, some managed to escape by paying Croats at the checkpoints, and what is also important in that period was that the Muslim property was looted and cars, tractors. And when the refugees, the Croat refugees from Fojnica came, Muslims had to move from their homes and some Muslims had been moved to the territory by the checkpoint of the HVO and then moved to the territory controlled by the Bosnian army, and some Muslims had to either move to their summer cottages or moved in with their relatives, whose houses had not yet been damaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dozic, let me ask you some points to clarify what you just testified about. When you say there were thefts of vehicles, who was stealing the vehicles and who were the victims of the theft?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the victims of the thefts were, of course, the Muslims, people from Duhri and the culprits were the soldiers of the HVO because they knew who owned cars. They would come to the homes and ask for the keys from the owners and take over the cars and the tractors without a word of explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the owners of those cars and the owners of the tractors ever given any receipts by the soldiers who took their cars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of the victims of those thefts ever given any compensation by the HVO soldiers who took their cars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my knowledge, as far as I know, no one had been compensated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the HVO ever return any of the cars that they had taken from the Muslims in your community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you testified about evictions in your community. Can you tell the Judges who was being evicted and who was doing the evicting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslims were being evicted and this was done by the soldiers of the HVO to come to their property, to their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would happen to the Muslims who were being evicted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were taken to the checkpoints and then they had to go to their relatives or to whatever place they could get to, but they were left to their own devices, as it were, once they passed the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the people who were being evicted notified well in advance so they could gather their personal effects and collect their personal effects before they left their homes, or were the circumstances different than I've just described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends. Sometimes they did have enough time, sometimes they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges the effect of those expulsions on the Muslim population in your Dzemat by June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they felt insecure, the insecurity was greater daily because no one could guarantee them any safety. Their life was very cheap. They could be killed by anyone and the killers would not be held accountable. So fear was very much present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Numerically, what affect did it have on your Dzemat. You said initially in your testimony that the population within your Dzemat was 600. By June of 1993 as a result of the expulsions, can you tell the Judges what the population of Muslims within your Dzemat was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was halved, about 300 were left in my Dzemat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dozic, you and I have talked about your giving an answer in a narrative form, and what I would like you to do is, in your own words, and in a narrative form, tell the Judges, please, what happened in your Dzemat after the events of June the 12th, after the date of the attacks on Tulica. Can you tell the Judges in your own words, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The events which occurred in these villages on June 12th and the events in Visnjica and Rotilj, Gomionica, while we could see the fire, we could see the smoke, we heard the firing, the shells and so on. The information we received the following day was horrible. There were women raped, killed, persecuted. In the evening we were in a field, we were cutting the grass, and we saw the soldiers of the HVO with the arrested Muslims, captured Muslims. After those events of the Muslims from my Dzemat, the HVO ordered that the arms should be surrendered and they followed that order and gave up their weapons, basically hunting guns, pistols, and some bombs. A few days later one morning, between 5.30 and 6.00, I was woken up by the bell ringing on my door. I went out and I saw two HVO soldiers who told me I had five minutes to get ready and to go in front of the mosque. I did as they told me. I got ready, and on the way to the mosque, I saw that most of the men from my Dzemat were moving towards the appointed place. There were about a hundred of us gathered there from my Dzemat, all men from 18 to 65 years of age had been rounded up in front of the mosque. After that, we were ordered to get onto trucks which were there, which had been brought there, and we were driven to the Kiseljak barracks. We were put up in three or four rooms in the first building as you pass the gate. We stayed there for two and a half to three hours. No one told us why we had been arrested. The room that I was in with a group of people, I came across two of my followers from my Dzemat, an elderly man of about 50 had been badly beaten, and with him was a young boy of about 15. He, too, had been beaten up, but not so severely. We asked them how it had happened, and they explained that that night they had wanted to cross into free territory, and the BiH army control, that they had been captured and brought that night there and beaten up. After two and a half to three hours, we were ordered to go out and to get on the trucks again, which we did, and we were then driven in front of the municipality building in Kiseljak. That building used to be used as the town hall before this event. We were ordered to get off the truck and to go into the building. The building was empty. It had two floors so that when we got in, we were put in the dormitories where we stayed from then on in groups. There were no beds, no blankets, so that we would usually put some paper on the floor and there was plenty of it in the municipality building, and we would take documents and use them as a pillow under our heads. What made things worse was that in the building there was no regular running water, and the toilets were mostly blocked up. During my stay of nine days in this building, never for a moment did any representative of the authorities inform us why we were there. On the second day, towards the evening, two HVO soldiers came in and asked that a group of people step out, a group of 30 to 35 men. The people were a bit confused. Then they started shouting, cursing. Some people were hit, kicked, some with rifle butts, so that after that, a group of 35 men was formed and they were boarded on a truck. When they came back the next day in the morning, talking to them, we had learned that they had actually been taken to dig trenches along the defence lines of the HVO facing the BiH army. After that, having realised why we were there, we decided that the existing 100 men should be divided into two groups so that one group would be working at night and the other group during the day. These men mostly went to dig trenches at all the places where the HVO had a confrontation line with the BiH army, above Kazagici, Vares, Duhri, Lepenica, towards the Fojnica municipality and so on. During my nine-day detention, I was not taken to dig trenches because the members of the Dzemat said, you are our Imam and you will not go, so that we learned about what happened to them there from what they told us. On the first day, we were given nothing to eat, and on the second our women were allowed to bring food from home. Then they brought us blankets and a change of clothing. During my nine-day stay there, we were visited by Mr. Borjo and Mr. Takan who was the president of the Red Cross in Kiseljak. On that occasion, we asked to be registered as prisoners by the International Red Cross. I think that, indeed, happened, though I was not there then. Nine days later, I was released from this detention, so I spent the rest of the time at home. A policeman who brought me home told me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there because I have some questions to clarify your narrative before we get into the next testimony, Mr. Dozic. You said that approximately 100 Muslim civilians were kept in the municipal building and the question I would like to ask you is: During the approximately nine days that you were there, were all of those Muslim civilians, with the exception of you and, perhaps, a few others, forced to dig trenches every day, every night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, each one in his shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, were you and the others who were imprisoned at the Kiseljak municipal building free to leave that building at any time during the nine days that you were a hostage there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We couldn't leave because there was a guard in front of the main gate of the building, and only people who had to see a doctor could, under police escort, go to the medical centre and be treated there, after which they would be returned to the municipal building. That was the situation while I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the nine days that you were there, did anybody ever give you an explanation, any HVO authority figure ever give you an explanation of why you and the others were being detained in the Kiseljak municipal building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never did anyone explain to us why we had been detained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn that some of the people who had been detained in the Kiseljak municipal building and who had been taken to dig trenches were killed or wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Killings and injuries occurred after I was released. Two men were killed, one of them is Rasim Bulut whom I buried, and I know two men who were injured and both of them were after transferred to the territory under the BiH army control for treatment. The other man who succumbed to his injuries, his name was Emso Redo, I was not the one to bury him, though I was in Rotilj at the time, and I found this hard to bear because the man was buried without any proper burial rights and we don't know where he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Were they killed while digging trenches or was it an actual death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, they were killed while digging trenches. Rasim Bulut was killed by a stray bullet which came from the BiH army's side. That is what I was told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the other man was also wounded. On the same occasion, two HVO soldiers were wounded because of the accidental activation of a mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, it is ten past four. I have noticed that we still have to go through all that happened after his release. You have finished your questions regarding the period up to the 12th of June, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have one or two more questions, but I can postpone those until after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would prefer you to put them so that after the break we have just the last point, so as to try and release the Imam this evening. So please put the questions that you need to up to the period of the 12th of June briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dozic, you were released from the municipal building after nine days. How long were the other people who were incarcerated in the municipal building kept in that building before they were released, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depended. Some people stayed until October, but in mid-September, as far as I'm aware, the men who were still in the municipality building were transferred to Rotilj, and then they formed a labour squad that existed in Rotilj, and that was taken out daily to perform labour required by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've concluded this part of my examination. What I intend to do after we come back is have the Imam testify about what events occurred after his return to Duhri.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: After his release. We agree with your plan and your summary. We will have recess and resume work a little after half past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Have the accused brought in, please? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dozic, focusing your attention on the time period between the time of your release from the Kiseljak municipal building until the time you and your family and others were expelled from the village of Duhri by the HVO on the 9th of September, could you, in your own words, tell the judges what happened to you and other members of your Dzemat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After spending nine days in the municipality building, I was taken back home and I stayed there until the 9th of September, 1993 when, with my family and another 100 members of my Dzemat, I was transferred to the camp at Rotilj. Several incidents occurred in the meantime. The appropriation of Muslim property continued by HVO soldiers. As there were no more cars or tractors left, it was like the return of the livestock, so they would simply enter a stable, select the cow they liked, and take it away without paying any compensation to the owners. Then they would also take fodder from the fields which the Muslims had left there in June, having cut it and prepared it for their own cattle. Then also they took my car. It was the only car that still remained in the village, and it was taken by the HVO police. I was given a certificate, but they said that they were taking it temporarily. To this day, I have not received any compensation or damages for this car, nor was it ever returned to me. An event that caused a great deal of panic in my village was the rape of a 19-year-old girl which occurred at the beginning of August 1992. In the evening, three HVO soldiers came and they took --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. May I make a correction, before you start with that part of the narration? The record says "August of 1992"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1993, the rape occurred at the beginning of August 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to have interrupted you, but I needed to make that correction. Could you please continue, Mr. Dozic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three HVO soldiers came to the family home of this girl, and they treated the mother roughly who tried to resist them taking the girl and her younger sister, who was 14 years old. They hit the mother and locked her up in her family home from the outside. The two mentioned girls were taken to another Muslim house, which is about 300 metres away from their family home. Three hours later, the girls were returned. The older girl had been raped, the younger one had not. She had been raped by two HVO soldiers. The third soldier did not take part in the rape. The mother, the next day, complained to the police, and the police allegedly said that the perpetrator had been arrested and that he had been punished. We don't know whether that, in fact, occurred. This event particularly provoked fear among young women and girls, so that after that, not a single young woman or girl dared sleep in their own homes, but would usually go into the maize fields, the maize being very tall in that period, or they would sleep in the stables or in the woods. This situation continued until the exchange of the Muslim population with the Croats in the area of Lepenica that occurred later. On that occasion, we managed to transfer, more or less, all the girls and some of the elderly people to free territory and the BiH army control in this exchange, which was legally arranged. The pressure continued and the eviction of Muslims from their homes, and the Muslims had to gather together in a very small area. Living conditions became intolerable. Another event that occurred at the beginning of September shocked the Muslim people; namely, one night, about 11.00, I heard screaming and noise in a house 150 metres away from the house I was living in. As it was night-time, we didn't dare move around. We were afraid, and I learned the next day that a young woman had been raped in the presence of her father-in-law, who had been beaten up, and on whose forehead a cross had been tattooed. This young woman was raped in the presence of her five-year-old son by three HVO soldiers, natives of Travnik. The poor woman protested the next day against everything that had happened that night to UNPROFOR forces. UNPROFOR, again, in its turn, protested with the HVO authorities, and towards the evening, one of the police officers showed me the protest note addressed by UNPROFOR to the HVO authorities and asked me whether this was true. I said it was because I knew it had happened, and they promised on that occasion that a police checkpoint would be formed at the entrance to the village and that the HVO police would protect the Muslim people in my village. Let me just add that this police checkpoint had previously been formed after the first rape. It existed for a couple of days and then it was removed. We wanted to see that checkpoint at the entrance to our village the next day, but the HVO police appeared with a bus and a mini-bus, and they ordered us to pack the essentials within 15 minutes and to come to the buses. We did as we were ordered, and on that occasion, about 100 remaining inhabitants of Muslim religion living in that village were transported. While leaving our houses, the houses which had still not been expropriated, HVO soldiers moved in immediately with their families. I remember very well that my house was moved into by a man called Branko Lovic (phonetic) who came from Fojnica, and he moved in with his family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you some questions then to further clarify the events that took place during the time period we're talking about. When you came back from the municipal building, from your imprisonment there, were you informed by your wife and by others, other women in the village, that jewellery had been stolen from them by HVO soldiers? Can you tell the judges what you were told?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My wife told me that while we were detained in the municipal building, they were in a garage of my neighbour's across the road, and two HVO soldiers came while they were there and threatened them, insisting that they surrender all the jewellery they had on them. On that occasion, my wife's necklace, bracelet and a golden ring was taken away. The jewellery of the other women was also seized. This happened frequently. Money would be taken, jewellery, especially from people that they knew had means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me just a second. You said jewellery was seized. Was it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'll repeat it again. You said that the jewellery was seized. So it was not stolen, it was done almost officially. Somebody came and took them openly or was it stolen at night or without the owner knowing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. During the day, a soldier or two under arms would come and tell you, "Hand over whatever jewellery you have or money."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So it was done in almost an official way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say "official."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: By somebody coming to steal, somebody coming in the name of the law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but if somebody comes in the name of the law, he has to give you a certificate. He must have a document, but no one ever received any document or any material compensation for what was taken away from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, to clarify your testimony about the rapes that occurred of these young women who were in your Dzemat, were both of these young women Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come an occasion when two Serb soldiers came to your village, and can you describe to the judges the circumstances of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One day, in the morning, I went outside and I was surprised to see two Serb soldiers with fire hats and cockades on those hats, which are the insignia of the Chetniks, members of the Serb army. They asked me whether there was a woman in the village with sheep, that they wanted to buy sheep from that woman. And then my neighbour, Mustafa, joined in this conversation, and he happened to know one of these, and we were surprised to see members of the Serb army in our Dzemat. Of course, we told them where they could find the woman they were looking for, and, apparently, they took these six sheep from this woman and paid a minimum price for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also described a series of expulsions during that period of time, that is, expulsions of Muslims. Can you tell the judges who was doing the expelling of the Muslims from their homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (No translation).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm not getting a translation at all, Mr. President, in English, at least, and the court reporter is not getting it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. She forgot to switch on her microphone. Could the witness please repeat?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dozic, could you start your answer from the beginning, please, because there was no recording of your answer on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Expulsions of Muslims from their homes went on continuously from April until September 1993. Most frequently, HVO soldiers would come and tell the owners that they had so much time to collect their essential belongings and to leave their homes, which these wanted to move into. These expulsions were sometimes done in a rough manner and sometimes not. Sometimes people were given a little more time to be able to take more things with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you relate to the judges the events that you experienced when you were performing religious burial rites on some of the deceased Muslims in your community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While we were burying Rasim Bulut, whom I mentioned was killed while digging trenches, because the cemetery where we bury our dead was next to the Sarajevo to Kiseljak road, the soldiers who would pass by in their private cars would hurl insults at us, "Balija, another Turk less," and similar such insults. In a house that was close by to the cemetery, folk music would be played very loudly, as loudly as possible, and we found this very painful. This was a house where Filga (phonetic) and his group lived, the house of Kasim Emso (phonetic).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, following the events on the 9th of September when the buses came to your village and took you, your family and other Muslims out of the village, did any Muslims remain in the village after the 9th of September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that date, there was not a single Muslim left in my village, and the next day, there was not a single Muslim left within the Kiseljak municipality, except for the Muslims in the Rotilj camp, which means all the Muslims in the municipality of Kiseljak were gathered in one place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain in Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in Rotilj for about one and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no additional questions. I've concluded my examination. Mr. Dozic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon, for your efforts in presenting the summary and your questions, and I hope you were able to put all the questions you needed for your examination-in-chief. Now, Imam, as you know, you will be asked questions by Mr. Nobilo, who is one of the Defence counsel of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Dozic, good afternoon. As you have heard, my name is Anto Nobilo, and together with Russell Hayman, I represent General Blaskic, and we would like to elucidate some points regarding your testimony. You indicated the area of your Dzemat on this map. For the benefit of the transcript, can we say that it is true to say that your Dzemat is around the main road going through Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is the main road from Kiseljak to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In April in '92?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Until July 1992, how do you assess relations between the Muslims and Croats in your municipality or, rather, in terms of the Territorial Defence of the municipality; were they correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, until my departure in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us now proceed to the period after you left. In your Dzemat, an armed conflict occurred. You were not present, but you heard from your villages about it, so you testified about it. Could you tell us whether your villages told you what was the main cause for this armed conflict or incident to occur in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Allegedly, a barricade was the cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And who put up the barricade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslims, but I learned that this roadblock was removed, that there was a talk between representatives of the Muslims and the HVO, and it was agreed to remove the barricade and, in fact, it was. That is what I was told, and that the attack occurred after the barricade was removed. That is what I was told, but I cannot testify about that as I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said the Muslims put up the roadblock. Were they members of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know that this roadblock that intercepted the main highway was guarded by armed persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was told that it was removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But before it was removed, was it manned by armed personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was, but it was removed before the conflict. That is what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were you told before it was removed how many armed men were concentrated at that roadblock and, generally, in the area of your Dzemat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't inquire about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know that at the time of the conflict, Sead Sinanbasic, the main commander of the Kiseljak Territorial Defence, had in Topola, in the area of your Dzemat in the youth centre, his command post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you I wasn't interested in these things and I cannot tell you about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: During your examination-in-chief, you spoke about damage to houses by bullets, shells and shrapnel. Tell me, do you know whether anyone told you whether anybody personally, by hand, torched houses or was all the damage due to the shelling and the fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to what I was told, it was due to shelling and fire and that a lot of the incendiary ammunition was used, and the stables suffered, in particular, and an antiaircraft gun hit my house, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that some of the hamlets were intact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I could see passing by these were Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But the Muslim ones were damaged. We must slow down because of the interpreters. Were you told who was in those Croatian villages at the time of the conflict? Was the HVO in these Croatian hamlets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know where the line of fire was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you don't know the details. You said that there was only a reserve police force. Do you know that in Duhri there were 41 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers who were in Duhri were on the front-line at Koscani, and they would come home only when they were relieved, but they were not in Duhri. They held the line at Koscani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness, when you answer questions, please look at the judges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Regardless of where they were, do you agree with me that there were 41 soldiers of the BiH army that came from Duhri?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: During that first conflict in August 1992, did anyone evict Muslims from their houses, or did the Muslims remain after the conflict to live in your Dzemat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was informed that the majority of Muslims abandoned their homes for a few days, but after that, they returned to continue living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the examination-in-chief, you said that from November 1992 until April 1993, life was more or less normal, with the exception of the events of the checkpoints; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do I remember well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell me, is this statement true which I found in your first statement, that the looting at the checkpoints was mostly done by extremist groups of the HVO known as Maturice consisting of criminals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at checkpoints but in the village where I was staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So it is correct that the looting was done by criminals from Maturice?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, can I have the page reference on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Page 3 of the statement, somewhere in the middle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As far as possible, limit yourself to the examination-in-chief, Mr. Nobilo. I will be very strict about this. I do not remember this being referred to in the examination-in-chief, Mr. Harmon. Was it? I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness did speak about robberies in his village. I just asked who was behind them. It was mentioned, but the unit was not mentioned; but the witness did speak about it. In the examination-in-chief, the witness spoke about robberies in his village. My question was simply whether it was correct that this was done by members of the Maturice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: At the time, from November, I'm talking about November, before April '93 when the attack against the village occurred, in that period, from November '92 to April '93, did a single military unit of the HVO attack any village, as far as you know, in Kiseljak municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You also said that when Rotilj and the other villages were attacked on the 18th of April, '93, you heard the shooting, the shelling, et cetera. Your villagers panicked and started moving out. How many men left then, before these forcible evictions by the soldiers that you referred to afterwards? I'm talking about those who left of their own free will, driven by panic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We can talk about panic that occurred immediately after the event, but after the refugees, the Croats from Fojnica municipality came, and when the expulsions started, they were no longer voluntary, so we must include voluntary and forced expulsions. And until the events in July, about 300 Muslims left. This is including those who went of their own free will and those who were forced to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I understand. But could you please tell us how many went voluntarily and how many were thrown out by the people from Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now, we're talking about the eviction of the people of Fojnica. Were they just from Fojnica or from Kakanj and Vares as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first there were people from Fojnica, then from Kakanj, then soldiers, we called them Travnikanis, that is HVO soldiers who crossed through Chetnik territories to the area of Kiseljak. We saw buses bringing them in, and a Croat told us that they were coming, and they told us along which route they had come, and then they too started looking for houses for accommodation. So these three men from Travnik who raped the second-mentioned young woman were living about 30 metres away from her in a new house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could we say that all the people who came to your village to expel the local inhabitants were either from Fojnica, Kakanj, or Travnik, but they certainly were not local Croats, your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why would our neighbours evict us when they had their own houses to live in?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So is my conclusion correct, that you were not evicted by your neighbours but people coming from other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is important for us is that it was done by HVO soldiers, and it was the authorities who had to provide accommodation for them and not the Muslims because they had not expelled them from their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I understand what is important for you, but allow me something that is important for me. Please answer my question. All the people who settled in your village, were they outsiders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it true that when such a soldier evicted a Muslim family, a Croat family was already waiting to move in as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were various cases. There were houses that only soldiers moved into, and there were other houses in which the soldiers moved in with their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We're talking about vehicles, when you talked about thefts and seizure of your vehicles, in addition to your car, did the HVO soldiers take those vehicles for official needs of their units or did the HVO soldiers take those vehicles for their own private needs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I just know that they did not issue any certificate for those vehicles. I don't know what they used them for.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You were released after nine days. Is it true that the Croatian friar, Brother ^ Borjo, intervened to have you released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that he visited us and he promised to intervene. I don't know who it was that intervened for my release.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How long after his visit were you released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember exactly, but I know it was very soon afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Are you talking about Friar ^ Borja Pervin from Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know his surname, but as far as I know, he was working for the Caritas Humanitarian Organisation. He was in charge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it true that when you were released, a Croatian policeman told you not to move about too much because you may be attacked by Croatian extremists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was advised like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The second rape; you said that you were told they were arrested. Do you know about the -- for the first. What about the second rape? Do you know whether any criminal proceedings were undertaken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know because that family moved immediately to ^ Pales, and the next day, it was transferred to territory under BiH army control, I don't know by whom, but I know for sure that these three Croat soldiers afterwards committed rapes in Rotilj of an older woman who was never married, who was about 30 or 35 years old, and they were looking for her, in fact, when they raped this other young woman. She was hidden. They couldn't find her, and then they went to this young woman and they raped her.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that after the second rape, you said in the examination-in-chief, that the policeman promised to set up a checkpoint. Is it true that you and the other villagers asked the Croatian police to set up this checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course we did, in order to be safe, because after the first rape, such a checkpoint was put up and there were no such incidents in our village. But it didn't last for long. And very soon afterwards, this second incident occurred, and they promised that a checkpoint would be put up the next day again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we conclude that for you, at that time, the existence of an HVO police checkpoint meant greater safety?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And had such a checkpoint existed in your village, would you say that your village had been turned into a concentration camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were anyway in a concentration camp because you couldn't leave your village. Even in your own village, you were exposed to danger. Ever since April '93, you were not allowed to leave the territory of Kiseljak by regular means. In fact, as of April '93, the Muslims were in captivity in the municipality of Kiseljak because they were not able to leave the municipality, only with special permits through personal connections or risking going across front-lines or through no man's land, but the Muslims could not regularly pass through checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So from what you have said, we can conclude that the authorities of the HVO did not allow Muslims to leave the community of Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only with special permits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: These soldiers which you heard about who were captured, did you hear that they were drunk on that evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know at all. I don't know if they had been captured or what had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On page 4, in the second section from above, in the last row or before the last row, it says that you had been informed that they were drunk.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you came to Rotilj, what was the food situation in Rotilj? Was there enough food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, basically, yes. It was autumn and people had enough wheat, had enough potatoes, because we know what is enough under war conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it true that Fra Bozo brought food on behalf of Caritas, brought food to the village. What about medical aid, was that provided for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For medical assistance you had to apply to the checkpoint, at the entrance to Rotilj, if you wished to see a doctor and people would notify a day in advance and then they would be issued special permits. Unfortunately, on one occasion, an older Muslim woman who was dressed in the Muslim costume had been beaten at the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What I asked you was whether Fra Bozo brought food to the population on behalf of Caritas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, once he brought two truckloads of food which he divided up to the inhabitants during my stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And how long were you in Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A month and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you were to go for medical care, did you have a military escort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they went on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could they go to Kiseljak to buy food to go and buy things in shops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did, but it was at their own risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can I conclude from that that outside of Rotilj, there was a less safe situation than in Rotilj itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the notion of safety is a relative one, but if we compare, we can say that with some reservation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What can we say?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would ask that Mr. Nobilo permit the witness to finish his answer before the next question is asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Well, I shall repeat because the transcript is going slowly and I have to make certain breaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we say, regardless of the fact that you said that safety was a relative notion, was safety outside of Rotilj greater than in Rotilj itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Well, the reply -- there seems to be some mistake, so there's an exchange of notion, I would like to ask the question once again. Could you tell me whether safety outside Rotilj was lesser than the safety in Rotilj itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is all, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You would like to add something, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Dozic, you were just asked the question by Mr. Nobilo whether safety outside of Rotilj was less than inside of Rotilj. Can you explain to the judges the reaction of the Muslim people who were detained in Rotilj, what they're reaction was when the HVO uniform soldiers came into the village of Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I said that the notion of security is a relative notion, in Kiseljak, where we used to live with the Muslims, because there was fear amongst the Muslims. It was enough to see the car in which the HVO soldiers were and the Muslims would run off to their homes or to woods because fear prevailed. You never knew what would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And you're talking about Muslims inside the village of Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no additional questions. I would ask that Prosecutor's Exhibit 369, the map of the Dzemat, be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. The Defence agrees. Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Imam Dozic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would like to clarify a question which I asked you during the examination-in-chief. When you mentioned that jewellery was seized by the HVO soldier, I told you was that in the name of the law, and you told me no, we had no receipt, or nothing, I didn't mean was it legal. I meant was it done by the authority, in the name of authority, not by people coming from the back door and hiding to steal. The same thing would apply to the cars. Were the cars taken in the name of the law by the authority or were they stolen by people who were hiding from the authority? Was it clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll try and answer your question. The taking of property occurred during the daytime by soldiers wearing HVO uniforms. One or two men under arms would come knowing people with a car or a tractor. They would demand the keys and drive off. If this was the confiscation of material resources for them to issue receipts, but as we received no receipts, what conclusion can we make? Because we would often see those men, those soldiers, driving those cars as their own for private purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So it was privately done but in broad daylight and with no punishment of the authorities? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are not aware that anyone was punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The same thing with the cars and jewels, but you said for the rape, there was some kind of answer that people were punished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what we were told but we don't know what was actually done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And it continued whether there was passage through checkpoints or with no passage through the checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This checkpoint was removed. It existed for only a couple of days, and during the second rape, there was no checkpoint there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So it was done by HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that when you returned to the village, you found out that Muslim buildings and the facades were damaged, but not the Croatian buildings, and you also knew that some people were shot dead like Zijad, and so on. As far as the buildings are concerned, were the Muslim and Croat buildings side by side or were they in different parts, areas of the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Potkraj, they were side by side, and in the other two, Topola and Duhri, there were only Muslim houses. And I said that the Croatian village of Brnjaci is on the road towards Sarajevo next to the village of Topole.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you have an idea who it was done by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was told that it was done by HVO soldiers. I wasn't there so I can tell you only what I was told. I cannot give you firsthand testimony about that event. I would prefer somebody else to testify about it, who was on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now, you have been arrested and you spent some time in detention with other people. Were you chosen for your quality, you are an Imam and other people are, amongst the prominent people of society, or was it just collecting people? Did they aim at certain people who symbolise or were the symbol of authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you listen to my testimony, I stressed that all military-aged men, regardless of their occupations, from 18 to 65 years of age were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And sent also to detention. And some of them were beaten up. Why were some of them beaten up? Were they resisting? Were they fighting back or was this just some kind of customary attitude?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regarding the beating that I described, that applied to the two men who are also from our village and who were already there when we came. From our group, a couple of men tried to hide when they called them out and, as a result, they were hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And you mentioned, this is my last question, you mentioned that two Serb soldiers came in and went to buy sheep and paid little money for it and so on. Was it possible for Serbs to come in? Were they allowed by the HVO to come in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, from what I said, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You don't know how they came in? They came in as soldiers or they came in in hiding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As soldiers wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Soldiers in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and with a typical insignia of the Chetniks, a special group of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And they walked around and were not arrested by the HVO in broad daylight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Thank you, Imam Dozic. I have no additional questions for you. You have been very helpful. I hope that regarding your spiritual community and all the damage you suffered, this must have been a very cruel period for you. You will be accompanied out and the Tribunal wishes to convey its wholehearted gratitude to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I take advantage of this opportunity, to thank you too for hearing me out, and I wish you every success in your future work. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, where do we stand now, if we wish to finish at the end of Friday morning, as the closed session with the Defence, tomorrow afternoon, will not, perhaps, last all afternoon, so I would like to know where we stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have two witnesses remaining, and I believe we'll be able to conclude with those witnesses by either tomorrow or Friday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Everybody must be tired by now, so perhaps we're going to have ten minutes grace period and we will resume work tomorrow at 10.00. Do you think we can finish with one of the witnesses tomorrow morning and with the other on Friday morning? I don't know how many hours you have envisaged for each.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We may even be able to finish with two tomorrow, but we will certainly be able to finish with one tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. Mr. Registrar, we started with the Imam at 3.30, so roughly how much is this for the Prosecutor? Everybody, I think, has tried to be concise. I thank you, Mr. Nobilo, I thank you, Mr. Harmon. I hope that this has not upset anyone. The Defence was able to express themselves, so was the Prosecutor, so were the judges, so this was a witness who took about one hour and forty five. That is roughly the average, we should try to observe so that both the Prosecution and the Defence are able to do their work. Without wishing to limit your time, that is not at all our intention, I hope you understand my concern. Are your future witnesses protected witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At least one of them is, Mr. President. I don't know about the second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. My last practical question, Mr. Registrar. Are we working in the same courtroom tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUBUISSON
utterances.text: In this hall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And we meet tomorrow at 10.00 in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
